question:
Let $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be defined as

$f(n) = \text{number of digits in } n \text{ (in decimal representation)}$.

Is $f$ one-one? Is $f$ onto? Give a detailed justification.
explanation:
Step 1: One-One

If $n_1 \ne n_2$ but both have same number of digits, then $f(n_1)=f(n_2)$. For example, $12$ and $99$ both have $2$ digits: $f(12)=f(99)=2$.

Thus, $f$ is not one-one.

Step 2: Onto

Is $f$ onto $\mathbb{N}$? For any $m \in \mathbb{N}$, choose $n=10^{m-1}$ (for $m \geq 1$), which has $m$ digits. Thus, for every $m \in \mathbb{N}$, there exists $n$ with $f(n)=m$.

Thus, $f$ is onto.

Conclusion:

$f$ is onto but not one-one.
